Summary

Validation ensures the model’s parts mathematically check out. Benchmarking asks whether emissions and economic data line up with real-world conditions, by comparing our direct emission factors to independent sources.

Both 

Validation and quality assurance and benchmarking feed the same loop into the next release: build → validate → benchmark → investigate → methodology change.

To benchmark our model, we compare direct emission factors to independent sources. We usually do not benchmark full supply chain (cradle-to-gate) factors as matching scope across sources is much harder.

Direct factors, not full supply chains

The comparisons on this page are about what each sector emits itself (D), not the full upstream intensity (N).

Prefer like-for-like denominators

The strongest comparisons already look like emissions divided by national-accounts output. Estimates built from a market price or a company’s revenue are different objects unless they are restated to match that same scope and denominator.

Sharper benchmark — The comparison isn’t quite like-for-like in scope or assumptions, so we adjust the external number to match what the model measures.

Model improvement — The gap points to a place to improve the model (for example, bringing in additional data).

Documented, valid difference — The model and the benchmark are measuring different things on purpose; we maintain the model and record why they diverge.

Note

These three outcomes are the point of the exercise. Benchmarking is not a single pass/fail score for the whole model.

bedrock is an open-source pipeline that builds the U.S. components of the model. It brings together the U.S. methods of USEEIO and CEDA. It produces the Cornerstone nowcast Make and Use tables for 2017 to 2024 on BEA’s 2017 detailed schema, along with the U.S. direct requirements, GHG extension, margins and price indexes listed above. Every methodology choice is set in a configuration file, so the effect of each choice can be tested on its own, and the results of each release are pinned so they can be reproduced exactly. The code is publicly available on GitHub under the Cornerstone Data Pipeline Attribution License, which requires attribution when it is used.

The ceda pipeline builds the rest of the global multi-regional model and produces the published emission factors. It takes the U.S. components from a pinned bedrock release, adds the IO tables and emissions for the Tier 1–3 countries, and maps them to the 405 common sectors with 

ABSR. It then links countries through bilateral trade, balances the multi-regional table with 

RAS, and solves for the total requirements. From that, it calculates the emission factors (including regional and global averages, price-year and purchaser-price variants, and margin factors) and writes the release files (see 

Calculating the emission factors). The pipeline grew out of the code behind CEDA and is maintained by Cornerstone. It is currently closed-source.

Both pipelines are tested automatically on every change, and their main outputs are compared with pinned reference results. See 

code validation.

Key assumptions

Data-year emissions describe current production

Assumption: Each country’s emissions from its data year still describe 2024 production.

Why we make it: Emissions data by sector, matched to each source’s IO sectors, are published with a lag, in some cases of several years.

How it affects results: Where emissions per unit of output have fallen since the data year, for example as electricity grids get cleaner, factors may be too high. The gap is largest for South Korea and Tier 3 countries (2018) and for Japan and ICIO countries (2020).

ICIO countries take the U.S. gas mix

Assumption: For ICIO countries, the split of each sector’s CO₂e total into gases follows the U.S. mix for that sector.

Why we make it: The OECD data give only total CO₂e by industry.

How it affects results: Total CO₂e for each sector is unchanged, but results by gas are less reliable. Where a country’s methane or fluorinated-gas share differs from the U.S., for example in rice farming, gas-level results could be off.

EDGAR-based FIGARO countries are re-split with CEDS

Assumption: For the 10 FIGARO countries whose emissions Eurostat estimates from EDGAR, CEDS gives a better split between mining, refining, and power and gas utilities.

Why we make it: EDGAR merges some activities that CEDS keeps separate, such as public power plants and on-site generation, and refining and extraction.

How it affects results: The split between these industries changes, but the country’s total for the group is unchanged.

Tier 3 countries share one set of proxy emissions

Assumption: Tier 3 countries share one pattern of direct emission intensities. They differ only in their overall level, set by fossil CO₂ per unit of GDP, and in their electricity intensity.

Why we make it: These countries have no emissions data by sector.

How it affects results: Differences between Tier 3 countries in which sectors emit the most are not captured, and non-CO₂ gases are scaled with fossil CO₂. Factors for these countries carry more uncertainty than those for Tiers 0 to 2.

Summary

The GHG extension attaches each sector’s own greenhouse gas emissions to the IO model, as CO₂-equivalent emissions of each gas per dollar of output (B). Every country follows the same steps, but the emissions data behind them, and how much detail they carry, depend on the country’s tier.



Figure 1:From source emissions to direct emission intensities (B). Every country follows the same steps; step 4 is needed only where a source does not separate every gas.

The IO model traces the dollars that flow through supply chains. The GHG extension adds what each sector emits while making its output. For each country and sector it records:

Emissions (E): the emissions of each gas by the sector in a year, in kilograms of CO₂-equivalent.

Direct emission intensities (B): those emissions divided by output, so kilograms of CO₂-equivalent of each gas per dollar of output.

B holds direct emissions only: what the sector emits from its own fuel use, processes, and other activities. Emissions from the sector’s suppliers come in through the supply chain (

L), not through B. For example, the emissions from generating electricity stay with the power sector, and other sectors’ purchased electricity reaches them through L.

Each gas is weighted by its global warming potential as its emissions enter the model, so E and B are already in CO₂-equivalent and no separate weighting step is needed. Adding up the gases in B gives the direct emission factors D (see 

Notation cheat sheet).

B has a row for each of seven gases or gas groups: carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF₃).

Each gas is converted to CO₂-equivalent as its emissions are loaded, with 100-year 

GWPs from the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) 

Forster et al., 2021. Methane is valued two ways: fossil methane, from fuel production and use, at 29.8, and non-fossil methane, from farming and waste, at 27.0. Fossil methane is valued higher because, once it breaks down, it leaves CO₂ that was not already in the atmosphere.

Several sources report emissions as CO₂-equivalent using older GWPs from the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) 

Myhre et al., 2013. These are converted to AR6, gas by gas.

B covers emissions from producing goods and services. Some emissions in national inventories do not come from a producing sector, and they are left out:

Household direct emissions. Fuel burned in homes and in personal vehicles is emitted by households, not by an industry, so it is not in B.

Land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF). National inventories, following IPCC guidelines 

Eggleston et al., 2006, report farming and LULUCF as separate sectors. Farming emissions are counted, in the farm sectors: methane from livestock and rice, N₂O from agricultural soils, CO₂ from liming and urea, and methane and N₂O from burning crop residues in the field. The LULUCF sector is not counted. This leaves out changes in the carbon stored in forests, soils, and other land, including CO₂ removed from the atmosphere, along with emissions from flooded lands and from forest and grassland fires.

Emissions data are compiled on one of two bases, and the model uses each source as published:

Territorial basis: emissions that occur within the country’s borders. National GHG inventories use this basis, and so do the U.S. and China data.

Residence basis: emissions by the country’s resident businesses, wherever they occur. Air emissions accounts use this basis, as do the 

FIGARO and 

ICIO emissions data. Emissions from a country’s airlines and shipping companies abroad are counted for that country.

The residence basis matches how IO tables define a country’s economy, so it suits an IO model. The two bases differ most for countries with large international transport fleets or many visitors. See 

GHG data by country tier for the basis of each source.

Every country’s emissions go through the same steps:

Start from source emissions by source sector. Each source reports emissions on its own sector list, which can be anything from hundreds of activities (the U.S. inventory) to 50 industries (ICIO).

Split broad sectors where better data exist. Some sources lump together sectors with very different emissions, such as electricity, gas, and heat, or all of farming. Where other data can separate them, the broad sector is split first, keeping its total.

Allocate to the common sectors. For the U.S., each inventory activity is allocated to the industries that emit it. For other countries, each source sector’s emissions are allocated to the matching common sectors with 

ABSR, weighted by U.S. emission intensities. The country’s total for each source sector is kept.

Fill in missing gas detail. Where a source does not separate every gas, the missing split is taken from the U.S. mix for the same sector. This is not needed for the U.S., China, Japan, or the UK, whose sources cover all seven gases.

Convert to CO₂-equivalent with AR6 GWPs. Sources reported in CO₂-equivalent with other GWPs are converted to AR6.

Divide by output. Each industry’s emissions are divided by its output (x), then converted to commodities using market shares (who makes each commodity), giving B per dollar of commodity output (q). Emissions data years differ by country; see 

Data years.

GHG data by country tier gives the sources and how each step is done for each tier.

Key assumptions

U.S. intensities shape detail within each source sector

Assumption: Within each source sector, a country’s emissions are allocated to the common sectors in proportion to U.S. emission intensities.

Why we make it: Outside the U.S., emissions data come on far fewer sectors than the 405 common sectors, and the U.S. data are the most detailed available.

How it affects results: Each country’s total for each source sector is correct, but its split between detailed sectors follows the U.S. pattern. Where a country’s mix of processes differs from the U.S. (for example, a different steelmaking route), detailed sectors within the same source sector could be too high or too low.

Household emissions are excluded

Assumption: Direct emissions from homes and personal vehicles are not assigned to any sector.

Why we make it: They are not emitted in producing goods or services, so they do not belong in emission factors for purchases.

How it affects results: Totals in B are lower than national inventory totals. Emissions from fuel production for household use, such as refining, are still counted, in the producing sectors.

Mixed accounting basis

Assumption: Each source is used on its published basis, territorial or residence.

Why we make it: Converting between bases needs data on emissions by residents abroad and non-residents at home, which are not consistently available.

How it affects results: Transport emissions in particular may be counted differently for territorial-basis countries (the U.S. and China) than for the others.

Checks we run

Splitting and allocation keep each country’s source totals, so its total emissions in the model match its source data.

U.S. totals by gas match the national inventory.

Summary

The emission factors are the model’s total emission factors (N): the CO₂e emitted across the whole supply chain per dollar of each commodity, by the country that produces it. This page follows the calculation from the matrices of 

the IO model and 

the GHG extension to the published producer-price (PRO) and purchaser-price (PUR) factors for each year.



Figure 1:From the model matrices to the published factors. The base calculation is in 2024 dollars; each year’s factors are re-priced from it. φ is the producer share of the purchaser price.

hierarchy.lvl2: From the model to total emission factors
From the model to total emission factors

records.content:
The IO model gives the total requirements L, the output needed from every sector in every country per dollar of final demand (see 

Total requirements (L)). The GHG extension gives the direct emission intensities B, the emissions of each gas a sector emits per dollar of its own output (see 

The GHG extension: overview). Each gas is weighted by its 100-year GWP from the IPCC AR6 as its emissions enter the model, so B is already in kg CO₂e per dollar, one row per gas (see 

Gases and global warming potentials). Adding up its rows gives the direct emission factors D, what a sector emits itself per dollar.

The total emission factors take one step: multiplying by L traces each sector’s direct emissions through every round of suppliers.

M = B × L gives the total emission factors by gas. A column of M gives, for $1 of one commodity from one country, the CO₂e of each gas emitted anywhere in its supply chain. These are the gas columns of the release.

N = D × L, which equals the sum of the rows of M, gives the total emission factors. This is the Total GHGs column of the release.

For the 65 countries in Tiers 0 to 2 and the rest-of-world region, L is solved once for the whole multi-region table, so M follows supply chains across every border in the table. Each column of N is one commodity produced in one country, so a factor describes where a product is made, not where it is bought.

The factors are per dollar of commodity output at producer price, in 2024 U.S. dollars, the model’s base year. They include every upstream supplier, but not the trade and transport services between the producer and the buyer, which are handled in 

From producer to purchaser price and 

Margin emission factors.

The direct emission factors D are part of the model but are not published as a separate table.

The 83 Tier 3 countries are not part of the multi-region table, so their factors are calculated one country at a time, from the proxy table and proxy emissions described in 

Tier 3: Proxy tables and 

Tier 3: Proxy emissions. Each country’s domestic inputs carry its own direct emission intensities through its domestic total requirements, (I − Adom)⁻¹. Its imported inputs carry China’s total emission factors from the multi-region table. The two parts are added to give the country’s M.

The release has a factor for each of 21 regions and one global average (GLOB). For each sector and each gas, a regional factor is the average of its member countries’ factors, weighted by each country’s output of that sector in 2024 dollars (q):

N_region = Σ (N_country × q_country) ÷ Σ q_country

Only countries in Tiers 0 to 2 have output data in the model, so Tier 3 countries are not included in the weighted average, even where they belong to the region. A region with no Tier 0 to 2 member uses the simple average of its members’ factors instead. The global average is weighted the same way over every Tier 0 to 2 country. The rest-of-world region is used only inside the model and is not published.

A few country–sector combinations have a total factor of exactly zero, because the source tables have no output or no emissions for that sector in that country. A zero factor would understate emissions for anyone buying from that sector, so it is treated as missing: the country’s factor is replaced by its region’s factor, or by the global average where the regional factor is also zero. The replacement applies to every gas.

hierarchy.lvl2: From the base year to each reporting year
From the base year to each reporting year

records.content:
Every source in the model is first brought to 2024 dollars: values are converted to U.S. dollars at the data year’s exchange rate and re-priced to 2024 with a U.S. price index (see 

IO sources by country tier). The model therefore produces 2024 factors, per 2024 dollar.

The factors for 2025 and 2026 are re-priced from the 2024 factors, sector by sector:

N_t = N_2024 × PI(2024) ÷ PI(t)

where PI is the sector’s price index and t is the year. When a sector’s prices rise, each dollar buys less of its output, so the factor per dollar falls. The emissions behind the factors are the same; only the dollar they are expressed in changes. Each year’s factors are therefore in current dollars of that year.

The price index is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis chain-type price index for gross output by industry (2017 = 100), mapped to the 405 sectors. The 2026 value is the average of the quarters published at the time of the release. Sectors without their own index keep a constant price. The same U.S. index is applied to every country, region and the global average.

A purchaser pays more than the producer receives: wholesale, retail and transport businesses add their margins on the way to the buyer. Each dollar at purchaser price therefore contains less of the product itself. The purchaser-price factor converts the producer-price factor to this larger dollar:

N_PUR = N_PRO × φ, where φ = 1 ÷ (1 + Σ A_margin)

Here A_margin holds the margins paid on each commodity, in dollars of margin per dollar of the commodity at producer price, one row per margin sector, and φ is the producer share of the purchaser price.

Margins come from the U.S. A_margin is built from U.S. margin data, on the industry-average margins paid by industries and business investment. The same φ is applied to every country, region and the global average (see the 

key assumptions for the IO tables).

Services and electricity have φ = 1. They carry no trade margins, so their producer- and purchaser-price factors are the same.

Each year has its own φ. The margin coefficients are re-priced to each year with the price indexes of the margin sector and of the commodity, so φ changes slightly from year to year.

The purchaser-price factor covers the emissions of making the product only. The emissions of the margin services themselves, such as running warehouses, stores and trucks, are not added to it; they are prepared as separate 

margin emission factors.

Published factors are rounded to three significant figures. Total GHGs is rounded from the unrounded total, so it may not equal the sum of the rounded gas values.

Key assumptions

2025 and 2026 factors reflect price changes only

Assumption: The supply chains and emission intensities of the 2024 model also describe 2025 and 2026. The factors for those years differ from 2024 only by the change in each sector’s price.

Why we make it: Input-output tables and emissions data for 2025 and 2026 are not yet available for any country.

How it affects results: Real changes after 2024, such as a cleaner electricity grid or a shift in where inputs are bought, are not captured in the 2025 and 2026 factors.

One U.S. price index for every country

Assumption: Each sector’s U.S. price change applies to that sector in every country.

Why we make it: Consistent sector-level price indexes in U.S. dollars are not available for every country and year.

How it affects results: Where prices in a country moved differently from U.S. prices, or its exchange rate against the dollar changed, its factors for 2025 and 2026 could be too high or too low.

U.S. margins in purchaser prices

Assumption: The U.S. share of trade and transport margins in each commodity’s purchaser price applies in every country.

Why we make it: Margin data comparable to the U.S. tables are not available for every country.

How it affects results: Where a country’s margins differ from the U.S., its purchaser-price factors could be too high or too low. Producer-price factors are not affected.

Gross-output weights for regional averages

Assumption: A region’s factor for a sector is the average of its member countries’ factors weighted by their output of that sector, using only countries in Tiers 0 to 2.

Why we make it: Output is the best available measure of how much of a sector’s supply each country provides, and it is available only for countries with IO tables.

How it affects results: The regional factor reflects the region’s largest producers. Where a region’s Tier 3 members produce differently from its Tier 0 to 2 members, their purchases are better represented by their own country factors.

Summary

Margin emission factors give the emissions of the wholesale, retail and transportation services that deliver a good from its producer to its buyer, per dollar of purchaser price. They are prepared for U.S. commodities only, for each year, and can be added to the U.S. purchaser-price factors when those delivery emissions are not counted elsewhere in a footprint. They mainly serve former USEEIO users, whose factors had a margin component.



Figure 1:A purchaser dollar pays for the good and for the services that deliver it. The purchaser-price factor covers the first; the margin factors cover the second.

Between the producer and the buyer, most goods pass through wholesalers, retailers and transport companies. Their charges are the trade and transport 

margins, and they are part of what the buyer pays: the purchaser price is the producer price plus the margins.

The 

purchaser-price factors spread the emissions of making a good over this larger purchaser dollar, but they do not add the emissions of the margin services themselves. Those emissions come from running warehouses, stores, trucks, trains, ships, aircraft and pipelines, and they are what the margin emission factors measure.

For each U.S. commodity j and each margin type, the margin emission factor adds up, over the margin sectors i of that type, the margin paid to each sector times that sector’s total emission factor:

Margin EF[j] = φ[j] × Σ N[i] × A_margin[i, j]

A_margin[i, j] is the margin paid to margin sector i per dollar of commodity j at producer price.

N[i] is the U.S. total emission factor of margin sector i at producer price, the same factor published in the PRO table. It includes the margin sector’s whole supply chain, such as the fuel a truck burns and the electricity a store uses.

φ[j] is the producer share of the purchaser price of j (see 

From producer to purchaser price). It converts the result from per producer dollar to per purchaser dollar, so the margin factor is on the same basis as the purchaser-price factor it is added to.

The margin sectors are grouped into three types:

Margin type

Margin sectors

Wholesale

The 10 wholesale trade sectors (423100, 423400, 423600, 423800, 423A00, 424200, 424400, 424700, 424A00, 425000)

Retail

The 9 retail trade sectors (441000, 444000, 445000, 446000, 447000, 448000, 452000, 454000, 4B0000)

Transportation

Air (481000), rail (482000), water (483000) and truck (484000) transportation, and pipelines (486000)

The total margin factor is the sum of the three types. Services and electricity pay no margins, so their margin factors are zero.

A_margin is built from U.S. margin data on the margins paid by industries and by business investment. Margins on household purchases and on changes in private inventories are not included. Because most retail margins are paid by households, the retail margin factors are close to zero for many goods.

The margin factors are prepared for each year of the release, 2024 to 2026. Each margin coefficient is re-priced from 2024 with the price index of its margin sector and the price index of the commodity:

A_margin,t[i, j] = A_margin[i, j] × (PI_i(t) ÷ PI_i(2024)) ÷ (PI_j(t) ÷ PI_j(2024))

and the margin sectors’ factors N for the same year are used, re-priced as described in 

From the base year to each reporting year. Each margin sector is re-priced with its own index.

The margin emission factors are published in their own workbook, with one tab per year ({YEAR}PUR). Each row is one U.S. commodity, with the columns:

Column

Meaning

Code

Good or service code, as in the emission factor tabs.

Name

Name of the good or service.

Location

USA.

Location Name

United States.

Total Margin

Sum of the three margin types, in kg CO₂e per USD at purchaser price.

Wholesale

Wholesale margin emission factor, in kg CO₂e per USD at purchaser price.

Retail

Retail margin emission factor, in kg CO₂e per USD at purchaser price.

Transportation

Transportation margin emission factor, in kg CO₂e per USD at purchaser price.

Add them only to purchaser-price factors. A U.S. purchaser-price factor plus the total margin factor gives the emissions of making and delivering a good, per purchaser dollar. Producer-price factors are per producer dollar and exclude the margins, so margin factors should not be added to them.

Avoid double counting. If you account for transport and distribution separately, for example in Scope 3 category 4 (upstream transportation and distribution), do not add the margin factors as well.

U.S. only. Margin factors are prepared only for U.S. commodities, because margin data are available only for the U.S.

The USEEIO Supply Chain GHG Emission Factors were published per purchaser dollar, as factors without margins, margin factors, and factors with margins, the sum of the two 

Ingwersen, 2024. In Cornerstone EEIO, the U.S. purchaser-price factors correspond to the factors without margins, and adding the total margin factor corresponds to the factors with margins.

Key assumptions

Industry-average margins

Assumption: The margins on each commodity are the average margins paid by U.S. industries and business investment.

Why we make it: The factors are designed for purchases by organizations, and household margins, mostly retail, are much higher than those businesses pay.

How it affects results: Where an organization buys goods at retail, its actual margins are higher than those in the factors, and the margin factors, especially for retail, understate the emissions of delivery.

U.S. margin sectors and margins

Assumption: The margin factors use U.S. margins and the U.S. factors of the margin sectors.

Why we make it: Margin data comparable to the U.S. tables are not available for other countries.

How it affects results: The margin factors describe delivery within the U.S. They are not prepared for other countries, whose distribution networks and transport modes can differ.

Summary

This guidance walks you through how to apply the emission factors to your corporate carbon footprint. The factors are cradle-to-gate: they cover the emissions of producing a good or service up to the point where you buy it. They are typically used for Scope 3, categories 3.1 (purchased goods and services) and 3.2 (capital goods). They can also be used for category 3.15 (investments) to estimate financed emissions, using a company’s revenue as the proxy for spend, following PCAF’s guidance.

This user guidance covers two topics:

How to choose the right emission factor: the country, the year and the exchange rate.

How to choose between purchaser and producer price.

A separate page, 

Margin emission factors, explains how the margin emission factors are prepared, which is mainly of interest to previous USEEIO users.

Every emission factor is defined by a sector, a location, a year and a price basis. The steps below take you from a line in your spend data to the factor that fits it, and then to an emissions number.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 1: Match the purchase to a sector
Step 1: Match the purchase to a sector

records.content:
Find the sector that best describes what you bought, using the sector descriptions that come with the factors. Pick the sector for the final good or service you purchased. You do not add up factors along a supply chain, because each factor already includes the upstream emissions of that sector. A purchase of steel products, for example, already includes the emissions of making the steel.

Each sector is related to a commodity and follows the BEA standard classification. For crosswalks to other industry classifications such as GICS, NACE and ANZSIC, please enquire about the 

Watershed enterprise product.

Use the location where the good or service was produced. When you do not know it for every supplier, work down this hierarchy and stop at the first one you have:

Country of manufacture

Country of the supplier

Country of purchase

Country of your company’s headquarters

If a country has no factor of its own for that sector, use the regional factor for the country’s region, and use the global average only when neither is available.

Why country matters. The same sector can have very different emissions per dollar in different places, because of each country’s energy mix, the structure of its economy and its trade. The chart shows the 2026 producer-price factor for management consulting in six locations.



Figure 1:Emission factor for management consulting by location, 2026, producer price (kg CO₂e per USD). The United Kingdom is highlighted because it is used in the worked example below.

Applying one country’s factor to all of your spend would misstate the emissions of suppliers elsewhere. A supplier in China has a factor about eight times the US factor for the same sector. A model with global coverage lets you use the factor of the country where the work is done.

Use the factor year that matches the year of your spend. Each factor is expressed in dollars of its own year, so a 2026 factor applies to spend in 2026 dollars. The factors for different years are not interchangeable: the same sector and country has a different factor for each year.

If your reporting year is not the calendar year, use the factors for the calendar year that holds most of your data. If the data splits evenly between two years, use the newer factors. For example, a reporting year from April 2025 to March 2026 has nine months in 2025 and three in 2026, so it uses the 2025 factors.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 4: Convert the factor to your currency
Step 4: Convert the factor to your currency

records.content:
The factors are per US dollar. Convert either the factor or your spend to the same currency using the recommended exchange rate information.

Factor per unit of local currency = factor per USD ÷ exchange rate

Use the rate for the year of the spend, not the rate on the day you do the calculation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Worked example: consulting services in the United Kingdom
Worked example: consulting services in the United Kingdom

records.content:
A company paid £10,000 for management consulting services from a UK supplier in 2026. The 2026 factor for management consulting in the United Kingdom is 0.0449 kg CO₂e per USD, and the 2026 exchange rate is 0.74283 pounds per US dollar.



Figure 2:From spend to emissions. Look up the factor, convert it to pounds, and multiply by the spend.

To see the breakdown by gas, apply the same steps to the factor for each gas.

hierarchy.lvl2: Choose between purchaser and producer price
Choose between purchaser and producer price

records.content:
Each year has two sets of factors. The producer price factors value a good at what the producer receives. The purchaser price factors value it at what the buyer pays, which adds the trade and transport margins on the way to the buyer. The same purchase therefore has a larger dollar value at purchaser price, and each dollar carries less emissions.

If you are unsure, use producer price. Margins are hard to estimate globally, even for government statistical offices, and producer price is the more conservative choice, meaning it gives the higher emissions estimate for the same spend.

Your situation

Use

You are unsure what your spend includes

Producer price

You are buying off-the-shelf goods at retail, so what you paid includes the usual wholesale and retail margins

Purchaser price

You buy directly from the producer and account for transport and distribution separately in your footprint

Producer price

You buy a service

Either: the two sets give the same factor in most service sectors

The consulting example shows the last case. The management consulting factor for the United Kingdom is 0.0449 at both producer and purchaser price, because a service has no trade margin.

For goods, the choice changes the result. The 2026 factor for computers in the United Kingdom is 0.0814 kg CO₂e per USD at producer price and 0.0539 at purchaser price. In pounds, that is 0.1096 and 0.0726 kg CO₂e per £, so £10,000 of spend gives about 1,096 kg CO₂e at producer price and 726 kg CO₂e at purchaser price, a difference of about a third. Match the factor to the price basis of your spend data: if your invoice is what you paid at retail, pair it with purchaser price.

Every year, the releases will be publicly available in October. The emission factors are the primary data product of each release, covering 405 sectors across 148 countries, 21 regions and one global average. This page describes the emission factor workbook; how the factors are calculated is in 

Calculating the emission factors. To download the latest version, check out 

Zenodo.

The 2026-rc.1 emission factors are published as one Excel workbook that contains: a cover, a data dictionary, a producer-price tab and a purchaser-price tab for each year the data is available for, and five auxiliary tabs.

Description: cradle-to-gate greenhouse gas emission factors in kg CO₂e per USD, by good or service, location and year, in producer and purchaser price. Prices are in current-year dollars, so the dollar year matches the data year.

Summary

Short answers to the questions we hear most about Cornerstone EEIO 2026. Each answer links to the page with the full explanation. Cornerstone EEIO is the successor of USEEIO and CEDA, so many answers compare it with those models.

What is the Cornerstone Sustainability Data Initiative, and how does it relate to USEEIO and CEDA?

Cornerstone launched in August 2025 to bring USEEIO and CEDA together into one open, comprehensive dataset of Scope 3 spend-based emission factors. Cornerstone EEIO 2026 is the first release of that combined model. It is the continuation of both USEEIO v1.4 and CEDA 2025. Today Cornerstone is the home of 3 additional datasets: eGRID, the GHG EF Hub and Orbae. Learn more at 

cornerstonedata.org, and see the 

release candidate note for what is in this release.

What is changing compared with USEEIO and CEDA?

Three groups of changes:

A more current US economy that accounts for imports. US tables are rebuilt for every year from 2017 to 2024, manufacturing uses facility-reported emissions, and imports are modeled where they are made.

Newer data for Europe, the UK and China, and better gap-filling for other countries.

A validation process that feeds back into the model. Third-party benchmarks review the sectors behind about 50% of global emissions.

Examples with numbers are in 

What changed in the release candidate note. The full list is in the 

Change log. Side-by-side summaries are in 

Summary of changes vs. USEEIO and 

Summary of changes vs. CEDA.

Are the changes driven by methodology or by real-world change?

Both. Data updates reflect real-world change, such as new economic, trade and emissions data. Methodology changes reflect modeling improvements, such as modeling US imports by origin and the auto-balanced structural reflection (ABSR) method. See the 

Change log and, for the size of each driver, 

What drives the change for CEDA users and 

What drives the change for USEEIO users.

Why is it called a “release candidate”?

2026 is the first time CEDA and USEEIO are combined in one model, and the first time a time series is released. The two-phase release gives companies time to assess the impact on their most recent year of measurements while the time series is under development. The release candidate (2026-rc.1) is published on October 27, 2026. The full release (2026-v1), with the 2017–2026 time series and the model matrices, follows in early December 2026. See 

2026-rc.1 (Release Candidate).

Will the 2024–2026 factors change between the release candidate and the final version?

We don’t foresee significant changes, but some sector–country combinations could move because of improvements made while developing the time series. If you need numbers for reporting or rebaselining, wait for the final version. See 

2026-rc.1 (Release Candidate) for what to expect from the time series.

When is the next update?

Releases are published every October so companies can plan for them. The next, Cornerstone EEIO 2027, will be released in October 2027. Cornerstone EEIO 2026 will stay methodologically stable for at least five years, so you have a consistent basis to rebaseline and set targets. See 

Releases and 

Update cadence.

Did the sectors change?

Yes, slightly. Cornerstone EEIO uses 405 sectors, based on the BEA input-output commodity codes. When the USEEIO and CEDA teams reconciled their US models, they resolved the differences in sector definitions as follows.

Changes compared to USEEIO

Electric utilities are aggregated into one sector (221100). USEEIO split them across three.

Government and private transit are aggregated into one sector. USEEIO kept them separate.

Changes compared to CEDA

Waste is split into seven sectors. CEDA had a single waste sector.

Aluminum is split into primary and secondary sectors. CEDA merged them.

Home appliances are one sector, as in the BEA tables. CEDA had four.

See the 

model reconciliation section of the change log for all 18 differences.

Did the file format change?

Yes. The new release is different from open CEDA and from the USEEIO v1.4. See 

What's in a release for more details.

How much will my footprint change?

It depends on which sectors and countries your spend falls in.

Coming from CEDA 2025: global production-weighted factors fall by 23.3%. In a sample of 400 corporate footprints, the median company sees a 14% decrease.

Coming from USEEIO v1.4: US factors change by −0.8% overall. In the same sample, the median company sees a 1.3% decrease.

A small median can hide large moves in individual sectors, in both directions. See 

How do the emission factors change?, 

Summary of changes vs. CEDA and 

Summary of changes vs. USEEIO.

I was using CEDA or USEEIO. Do I need to rebaseline or restate previous years?

We do expect the majority of companies to be above the SBTi rebaselining threshold, but every company will have a different experience and ultimately whether to restate is a decision under your own company’s policy and your target framework. This year, the release of the time series is designed for exactly this purpose. Because every year from 2017 to 2026 is built with one methodology, you can recalculate prior years on a consistent basis and compare them. See 

2026-rc.1 (Release Candidate) for what to expect from the time series, and 

Summary of changes vs. CEDA and 

Summary of changes vs. USEEIO for how much your factors may move.

Can I keep using CEDA 2025 or USEEIO for 2026?

We recommend using Cornerstone EEIO 2026 for 2026 measurements, since it supersedes both. If you have a reason to stay on a previous version, apply a price index to it, and explain the choice to your verifier. See 

Summary of changes vs. CEDA and 

Summary of changes vs. USEEIO for what changed.

I’d like to explain the switch to Cornerstone in my report. What do you recommend?

State the source (Cornerstone EEIO 2026) and the years you are applying the model to.

Suggested wording: “The changes this year are due to adopting Cornerstone EEIO 2026. The Cornerstone model combines CEDA’s global coverage with USEEIO’s detailed US data into a single model that supersedes them both. This model was adopted as an improvement in data quality, as it provides a more current picture of the global economy.”

For numbers you can cite, see 

What changed in the release candidate note, 

Summary of changes vs. CEDA and 

Summary of changes vs. USEEIO.

How do I choose between producer and purchaser price?

The producer price is what the producer receives. The purchaser price adds trade and transport margins, and is what you pay for a ready-to-buy product. If you’re unsure, use producer prices, which are more conservative. If you’re confident your spend includes typical margins, for example buying off-the-shelf goods at retail, use purchaser prices. See 

Choose between purchaser and producer price.

How do I use the factors for goods bought from, or made in, another country?

Choose the country where the product was produced. If you don’t know it, use this order, from most to least relevant:

Country of manufacture

Country of the supplier

Country of purchase

Country of your company’s headquarters

If a country has no factors of its own, use its regional average. The Locations tab shows which of the 249 locations have their own country factors (148 do) and which region each belongs to. See 

Step 2: Choose the country.

What if my supplier is in a country with no data?

Use the factor for the region it belongs to, or the global average if the region isn’t clear. See the Locations tab, 

Methods by country and 

Step 2: Choose the country.

What do the Scope 3 categories cover?

The factors cover upstream emissions up to the point of purchase, so they apply to the upstream categories: purchased goods and services (1), capital goods (2), upstream transportation and distribution (4), waste generated in operations (5), business travel (6), and upstream leased assets (8), as well as the upstream part of category 3. They don’t cover downstream emissions (categories 9–15). See 

User guidance.

Why does the same sector have very different factors in different countries?

Three reasons: the emissions intensity of each country (for example its electricity grid), the economic structure of the sector in that country, and the trade structure, meaning where its inputs are imported from. Factors for a sector in countries with detailed data differ for real reasons, but see the tier question below for countries with less data. For worked examples, see 

New data for China and 

New data for Europe.

Are the factors suitable for GHG Protocol Scope 3 reporting and for target setting?

Yes. Cornerstone factors are designed for spend-based Scope 3 calculations under the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard, and they follow its minimum boundary conditions: a cradle-to-gate boundary that covers all upstream emissions up to the point of purchase, all seven GHGs reported in CO₂e with IPCC AR6 100-year global warming potentials, and no downstream emissions. See 

User guidance and 

The GHG extension: overview.

Does Cornerstone EEIO follow a cradle-to-gate boundary?

Yes. The factors cover all upstream emissions, from raw material extraction up to the point of purchase. Downstream use and end-of-life emissions are not included. See 

User guidance.

Does Cornerstone EEIO account for direct land use change and land management emissions?

The factors do not account for direct land use change, but they do include land management emissions. Farming emissions are counted in the farm sectors, including methane from livestock and rice, N₂O from agricultural soils, and CO₂ from liming and urea. Land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF), including carbon removals, is not counted. See 

What is and isn’t counted.

Does Cornerstone EEIO exclude any of the seven GHGs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, NF₃)?

No. All seven GHGs are included. The release reports each gas separately, alongside the total, in kg CO₂e per USD. See 

Gases and global warming potentials and 

Producer and purchaser price tabs.

Are biogenic emissions included in the factors?

No, biogenic emissions are not included.

Which GWP version is used?

IPCC AR6, 100-year time horizon. Sources that report in AR5 CO₂-equivalents are converted to AR6 gas by gas. Prior versions of USEEIO used earlier GWPs, so a share of the change versus those models comes from the GWP update. Cornerstone EEIO 2026 also fixes a double application of the AR5-to-AR6 conversion. See 

Gases and global warming potentials, the GWP tab described in 

Auxiliary tabs and the bug fixes in the 

Change log.

Cite the version and the release date. For example the Cornerstone EEIO 2026-rc.1 released on October 27th, 2026. See 

Cover and 

Releases.

What license are the factors under, and what attribution is required?

The factors are published by the Cornerstone Sustainability Data Initiative under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. You can use and redistribute them, including commercially, as long as you give credit and indicate any changes. Please attribute the factors to Cornerstone EEIO. See 

Cover.

What does a country’s tier mean for how much I can rely on its factors?

Countries are grouped in four tiers by the input-output data available for them. Tier 0 (US) has detailed annual tables, Tier 1 (China, Japan, South Korea, UK) uses detailed national tables, Tier 2 (60 countries) uses coarser multi-regional tables from FIGARO or ICIO, and Tier 3 (83 countries) has no usable table and uses a proxy table built from other countries. Factors for Tier 3 countries carry more uncertainty. See

Cornerstone EEIO is a continuation of the USEEIO and CEDA EEIO models, built from the best of each model as determined by the developers through

CEDA dates back to the early 2000s, when Sangwon Suh developed it, first at Leiden University and later at the University of Minnesota 

Suh, 2005.
It began as a U.S. single-region model with environmental extensions covering many environmental indicators.
VitalMetrics maintained it and applied it in private, public and academic work.
CEDA was expanded into a global MRIO model focused on GHG emissions before Watershed acquired it in 2023. Under Watershed, GHG emission factors for Scope 3 reporting became its primary purpose, and in 2025 Watershed released a free version of the emission factors as Open CEDA.

USEEIO was a research product of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA), first released in early 2017 and developed as a fully open-source model

Summary

An environmentally-extended input-output (

EEIO) model combines data of how outputs produced by sectors in an economy serve as inputs for other sectors along with environmental attributes of each sector. When the economic data is extended with environmental data this way, such as with GHG emissions, the resulting model can produce emission factors that represent the GHG emissions across a whole supply chain per dollar spent on a sector’s products.



Figure 1:An EEIO model combines input-output tables with an environmental extension to produce emission factors.

EEIO grew out of economic input-output analysis when economist Wassily Leontief added the pollution generated by each sector to his model of the economy 

Leontief, 1970, and it has been a basis for carbon footprinting of nations, organizations, and products over the last few decades 

Minx et al., 2009. Cornerstone EEIO continues two of the longest-running US EEIO models, USEEIO and CEDA; see 

Origins of the Cornerstone EEIO.

Each data component is put into a matrix, named by a letter that is common in input-output analysis and used throughout these docs (see 

Notation cheat sheet). Input-output analysis then combines the matrices with matrix algebra.

Input-output tables. The supply (V) and use (U) tables record which sectors produce which products, and which products each sector and final user buys. From them come the direct requirements (A), the inputs a sector buys per dollar of its output, and the total requirements (L, the Leontief inverse), which add up the purchases through every round of suppliers. See 

The IO model: overview.

Environmental extension. Emissions of each gas by each sector (E), weighted by each gas’s global warming potential to give CO₂-equivalent and divided by the sector’s output, give the direct emission intensities (B). See 

The GHG extension: overview.

Emission factors. Adding up the gases in B gives the direct emission factors (D), for what a sector emits itself. Combining them with the IO tables gives the total emission factors, N = D × L, for what is emitted across its whole supply chain.

An EEIO model has the same matrix structure as the models used for life cycle assessment (LCA) 

Suh, 2005. In both, a matrix of the inputs each activity needs is inverted to trace every upstream supplier, and a matrix of emissions per unit of each activity is multiplied through it. The difference is that EEIO describes sectors in dollars, where LCA usually describes individual processes in physical units. Because of this shared structure, EEIO data can serve as background data in LCA, as discussed in 

Ingwersen (2026).

A single-country model assumes imported products are made the same way, and with the same emissions, as products made at home. A multi-regional input-output (

MRIO) model instead links countries’ input-output tables through international trade, so each import carries the supply chain and emissions as it was produced in the origin country. For the companies reporting to the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP), in one study using an MRIO model instead of a U.S. single-region model raised their estimated upstream emissions by about 10% 

Davis et al., 2025. The Cornerstone model is an MRIO model; see 

From single-country tables to the multi-region model.

For a book-length introduction to EEIO and its use in LCA, see 

Hendrickson et al. (2006).

Key assumptions

Price basis does not change input recipes

Assumption: Countries publish their tables on different price bases (basic, producer, or purchaser prices, and sometimes a mix within one table). We use each table as published and assume these differences do not materially change the direct requirements (A).

Why we make it: Converting every table to one price basis needs product-level tax, subsidy, and margin data for each country, which is not consistently available.

How it affects results: Where product taxes or trade and transport margins are large, as for fuels, input coefficients could differ from those on a common price basis. See 

User guidance.

U.S. margins for purchaser prices

Assumption: Factors are converted from producer to purchaser prices using U.S. trade and transport margins for every country.

Why we make it: Margin data comparable to the U.S. tables are not available for every country.

How it affects results: Where a country’s wholesale, retail, or transport margins differ from U.S. margins, its purchaser-price factors could be too high or too low. Producer-price factors are not affected. See 

User guidance.

Tier 3 countries share one recipe

Assumption: Tier 3 countries share one proxy table input recipe. Each country differs only in its overall import share, applied equally to every sector, and in its direct emission intensities, which are scaled to the country’s emissions per unit of GDP, with its own electricity intensity. Their imported supply chains are approximated with China’s.

Why we make it: These countries have no usable published IO table.

How it affects results: Differences in industry structure between Tier 3 countries are not captured, and imports from countries other than China are given China’s supply chains. Factors for these countries carry more uncertainty than those for Tiers 0 to 2.

Summary

Cornerstone uses standardized national input-output tables to represent production recipes and link them with global trade data, thus representing domestic and international supply chains.

Every country enters the model as a national IO table, but countries don’t all start from the same kind of table. The first step is to collect the best available table for each country and record where it came from: the source, version, year, valuation, and sector detail. Which table we start from depends on the country’s 

tier: the U.S. starts from 

Make and Use tables for 2024 that Cornerstone produces using BEA’s methodology, after 

redefinitions and following BEA’s 2017 detailed schema, while other countries start from national statistical agency tables, 

FIGARO or 

ICIO, or a proxy table. See 

IO sources by country tier for what each tier starts from.

The detailed U.S. structure sets the model’s common sector list, and it is used to split other countries’ coarser sectors (see 

ABSR). Sector lists and currencies are reconciled in the later steps: mapping to the common sector list, linking with trade data, and balancing.

Figure 1:The Supply and Use tables. Supply shows who makes each commodity; Use shows who buys it and what each industry adds in value. The Make table (*) is a variant of Supply that leaves imports to the Use table.

An economy’s IO accounts come as a pair of tables.

Supply (V) records the production of each commodity by each domestic industry, plus imports of each commodity. The Make table, used for the U.S., is a variant: it has the same production block but no imports row. Imports appear instead in the Use table’s final demand, as a negative column. Either way, the production block gives two output totals:

Industry output x: the sum across an industry’s row, which is everything the industry makes, including secondary products.

Commodity output q: the sum down a commodity’s column, which is everything domestic industries make of that commodity. Adding imports gives the total supply of the commodity.

Use (U and y) records who buys each commodity:

Intermediate use (U): the commodities each industry buys as inputs.

Final demand (y): the commodities bought by final users, namely households, government, investment, and exports.

Value added: below each industry’s inputs, its wages, taxes on production, and profits.

The two tables balance. For each commodity, total supply equals total use. For each industry, inputs plus value added equal the industry’s output x.

Figure 2:The Use table is split into domestic and imported use, for industries and final users alike.

A purchase can come from a domestic producer or from abroad, and the two lead to different supply chains. So the Use table is split in two:

Domestic use (Udom, ydom): commodities bought from domestic producers.

Imported use (Uimp, yimp): commodities bought from producers in other countries.

U = Udom + Uimp. Final demand splits the same way, with exports on the domestic side: y = ydom + exports + yimp. Imported use is later traced back to the countries that made the imports, using trade data. How each country’s tables arrive at this split is described in 

IO sources by country tier.

Figure 3:Domestic and imported direct requirements are built from the same two steps.

The direct requirements tables turn the Supply and Use tables into recipes: the inputs needed to make $1 of each commodity. They take three steps.

Inputs per dollar of industry output. Divide each industry’s column of domestic use by its output x.

Market shares. Divide each commodity’s column of the Supply table by its output q. This gives the share of each commodity made by each industry.

Combine. Multiply the two to get inputs per dollar of each commodity. Doing this with domestic use gives Adom; doing it with imported use gives Aimp.

For more details on the math behind it, contact 

team@cornerstonedata​.org.

Adom and Aimp add up to the total direct requirements A. A column of A is the input recipe for $1 of that commodity, split by where the inputs come from.

Tables that are already symmetric, with the same sectors on rows and columns, skip step 2: their domestic and imported use are divided by output directly. This applies to the Tier 1 and Tier 2 tables.

Final demand in the Use table includes purchases of imports. To match domestic production, we need final demand for domestic products only. We call this ynab, the final demand for the national accounting balance: domestic final demand for domestic products (ydom) plus exports.

Here ydom is what households, government, and investment buy from domestic producers, and yimp is what they buy from abroad. Imports not bought by industries go to final users, so yimp is total imports less the row sums of Uimp. Exports are the country’s own production, so they count toward ynab in full.

With ynab, the model reproduces the country’s commodity output: running ynab through the domestic supply chain (the Leontief inverse of Adom) gives back q. This is a check that the tables, Adom, and ynab are consistent.

Figure 4:The 

MRIO direct requirements table. Each country’s domestic inputs sit on the diagonal; its imported inputs are spread down its column by country of origin.

Each country’s tables say how much of its inputs are imported, but not where they come from. The multi-region model links the countries so that a supply chain can be followed across borders.

Put every country in one table. The 65 countries in Tiers 0 to 2 each get their own block, so A is a 65 × 65 grid of country blocks, each 405 × 405 sectors. Each country’s Adom sits on the diagonal. A country’s column holds everything its industries buy; the rows say which country sold it.

Split imports by origin. Each country’s Aimp is spread down its column using bilateral trade data (

BACI): for each product, the share the country imports from each origin. Products the trade data don’t cover, mostly services, use origin shares from 

FIGARO or 

ICIO. Imported final demand (yimp) is split the same way.

Add the rest of the world. Imports from countries outside the table come from a rest-of-world region. Its domestic input structure is pooled from the tables of Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. It is added as one more block, making A a 66 × 66 grid of country blocks. This region is separate from the proxy table used for Tier 3 countries’ own factors (see 

IO sources by country tier).

Balance. The table is balanced with 

RAS, so that each country’s sales to all users, at home and abroad, add up to its output, without changing it’s domestic recipe. This makes small adjustments to the import coefficients.

Solve. The total requirements (L) are calculated for the whole table at once, so supply chains that cross several borders are captured in full (see 

below).

The other 83 of the model’s 148 countries (Tier 3) are linked to this table more simply; see 

IO sources by country tier.

A shows only a sector’s direct suppliers. Take $1 of furniture. Its column of A lists what the furniture maker buys to make it: lumber, hardware, electricity, transport. These are the first tier of the supply chain.

Each of those suppliers has its own column in A. The sawmill buys logs, fuel, and machinery; the power plant buys fuel and equipment. These purchases are the second tier. Each supplier’s column is scaled by how much of it the first tier needs: if the furniture maker buys 20 cents of lumber for each $1 of furniture, the sawmill’s whole recipe is multiplied by 0.20. The second-tier suppliers have their own suppliers, the third tier, scaled again by what the second tier needs, and so on, without end. In the multi-region model the trace crosses borders: a second-tier supplier may be a steel mill in another country.

Each tier is smaller than the one before, because every dollar of output pays for value added (wages, taxes, profits) as well as purchases. So the tiers add up to a finite total: everything produced, anywhere in the supply chain, to deliver $1 of each commodity to a final user. Written out, that total is I + A + A² + A³ + …, where I is the $1 of the commodity itself, A the first tier, A² the second, and so on.

There is a simple way to calculate this infinite sum all at once: a special inverse of A, (I − A)⁻¹, called the Leontief inverse after the economist Wassily Leontief. That is why the result is called L. A column of L shows the total output needed from every sector, in every country, for $1 of final demand for that commodity.

Note

The tiers here are rounds of suppliers in a supply chain. They are not the same as the 

country tiers, which describe the data available for each country.
### What the model can and can't trace

`L` follows supply chains through the 66 countries in the multi-region table. The 83 Tier 3 countries are not separate parts of that table, so supply chains can't be traced to them one by one.

| Question | Can the model answer it? |
|---|---|
| How much of a U.S. product's supply chain is in China, Germany, or Korea? | Yes. Each of the 65 countries has its own part of the table. |
| How much is in Kenya or Egypt specifically? | No. Imports from all Tier 3 countries are grouped into the rest-of-world region. |
| Do the emissions traced to the rest of the world reflect those countries? | Not directly. The region's input recipe and emission intensities come from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. |
| Where do a Tier 3 country's own supply chains lead? | Only to its own economy and to its imports as a whole, which are approximated with China's supply chains. |


Key assumptions

Industry technology

Assumption: An industry uses the same input recipe for everything it makes, its primary product and any secondary products alike. This is what lets the market shares (V ÷ q) turn industry recipes into commodity recipes.

Why we make it: It is the standard assumption for building commodity-by-commodity tables from Supply and Use tables, and unlike the alternative (commodity technology) it never produces negative requirements.

How it affects results: A secondary product takes on its producer’s recipe. Using U.S. tables after 

redefinitions keeps secondary products, and so this effect, small.

Import proportionality

Assumption: Within a country, every buyer of a product gets the same mix of origins. If a country imports 30% of its steel from Korea, every industry that buys imported steel gets 30% of it from Korea.

Why we make it: Trade data record which countries trade each product, but not which industry buys the imports.

How it affects results: An industry that in reality buys mostly from one origin gets the national average mix instead. Where origins differ a lot in emission intensity, this can move that industry’s factors.

The rest of the world looks like four proxy economies

Assumption: The rest-of-world region stands in for every country outside the multi-region table, including all Tier 3 countries, as a source of imports. Its input recipe and emission intensities are pooled from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. It buys nothing from other regions, so a supply chain that reaches it stays there.

Why we make it: Countries outside the table have no linked IO tables of their own, and these four are the lower-income OECD economies in the table.

How it affects results: Imports from Tier 3 countries carry the proxy economies’ emission intensities rather than their own. Supply chains can’t be traced to individual Tier 3 countries, or onward from the rest of the world to other regions.

Data-year recipes, shares, and intensities still apply in 2024

Assumption: The IO tables, emissions, trade shares, and gap-fill shares come from different years (for example, 2024 trade data with IO tables and emissions from 2018 to 2023). We assume the input recipes, origin shares, and emission intensities from each source’s data year still describe the 2024 economy. Each country’s emissions are divided by its output from the same year; that output is re-priced to 2024 dollars with a U.S. price index, so its direct emission intensities are data-year intensities per 2024 dollar.

Why we make it: National tables, multi-regional databases, and trade data are published on different schedules, and we use the most recent of each.

How it affects results: Where an economy’s structure, trading partners, or emission intensity changed between the data year and 2024 (for example, a cleaner electricity grid), the model reflects the earlier pattern. Using one U.S. price index for every country means price changes elsewhere are not captured. The years used for each country are listed in 

Methods by country.

ABSR

Auto-Balanced Structural Reflection. The method that expands a country’s coarser IO table onto the model’s common sector schema, using U.S. structure as weights, while keeping the country’s accounts balanced.

Basic price

The amount a producer receives for a product, excluding taxes on products and including subsidies on products.

BACI

The CEPII database of bilateral international trade by product, used to split each country’s imports by country of origin.

CEDS

Community Emissions Data System. A global inventory of emissions by country and detailed activity, used to refine the split of emissions between energy industries and for China’s CH₄ and N₂O.

Country tier

A group of countries modeled with the same level of detail and the same kinds of data sources: Tier 0, detailed annual IO tables (the United States); Tier 1, detailed periodic national IO tables; Tier 2, coarse multi-regional tables from FIGARO or ICIO; and Tier 3, no IO tables (a proxy table built from other countries).

EDGAR

Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research, from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre. Global emissions by country and activity; the basis of FIGARO emissions for its non-European countries.

EEIO

Environmentally-extended input-output model. An input-output model of an economy with environmental data (here, greenhouse gas emissions) attached to each sector.

FIGARO

Full International and Global Accounts for Research in input-Output analysis. Multi-regional IO tables from Eurostat and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, used for many Tier 2 countries.

GHGRP

EPA’s Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, under which large U.S. facilities report their emissions each year.

GWP

Global warming potential. The warming effect of 1 kg of a gas relative to 1 kg of CO₂ over a time horizon. The model uses AR6 values with a 100-year horizon.

Make/Use framework

IO tables that record which industries make which commodities (Make, or supply) and which commodities each industry and final user buys (Use).

Margin emission factor

The emissions of the wholesale, retail, and transportation services that deliver a good to its buyer, per dollar of purchaser price. Prepared for U.S. commodities only.

Margins

The trade and transport costs added between the producer and the buyer: transport, wholesale, and retail.

MRIO

Multi-regional input-output model. Country IO tables linked into one global system through international trade.

ICIO

The OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables, used for Tier 2 countries not covered by FIGARO.

Producer price

The basic price plus taxes on products, less subsidies on products, excluding margins.

Purchaser price

The price the buyer pays: the producer price plus trade and transport margins. The emission factors are published per dollar of both producer price and purchaser price.

RAS

An iterative method that scales the rows and columns of a table until it matches known row and column totals.

Redefinitions

Adjustments that move secondary products (and their inputs) to the industry where they are the primary product.

Residence basis

Emissions accounting that counts emissions by a country’s resident businesses and households wherever they occur, matching the boundary of national accounts and IO tables.

Structural reflection

Using a detailed table’s structure (here, the U.S. tables) as weights to split a coarser table into finer sectors.

Territorial basis

Emissions accounting that counts emissions occurring within a country’s borders, as national GHG inventories do.

Summary

The 2026-rc.1 (Release Candidate) is the first stage of a phased approach to releasing Cornerstone EEIO 2026, the successor of USEEIO and CEDA. It publishes the model’s primary data product: spend-based GHG emission factors, in kg CO₂e per USD, for 405 sectors across 148 countries, plus 21 regional averages and one global average. The factors are cradle-to-gate, use 2024 as the base year, and are available for 2024, 2025 and 2026 measurements.

This release candidate will be superseded in December by the full 2026-v1 release, which will include a time series of emission factors from 2017 to 2026 and will be accompanied by the model matrices, in a format still to be decided.

Download this release on 

Zenodo here.

Why have a Release Candidate?

2026 is an unprecedented year of development because it is the first time we are combining CEDA and USEEIO into one model and also the first time we are releasing a time series. The intention behind having a two phased approach to the release is to give companies additional time for impact assessments on their most recent year of measurements, while the time series is under development. This enables companies to understand footprint changes before applying the time series.

Will there be any changes for years 2024 to 2026 once the time series is released?

We do not foresee significant changes, but some sector-country combinations could be impacted by improvements driven from the time series model development. Users should consider this version as a release candidate and wait for the final 2026 version of this model that will be released in early December for reporting and rebaselining purposes.

What to expect from the time series?

The time series (2017-2026) will use the same methodology for all years and only change the underlying data that represents each country’s economic structure and emissions data. For example, in the US each year of the dataset will use the US electricity grid emissivity for each year, capturing any decarbonization on this sector year over year.

This is the first time that either USEEIO or CEDA releases a time series built this way. In the past CEDA has released a time series built with inflation adjustments for years prior and after the base year. Moving forward the Cornerstone EEIO will only apply inflation adjustments to the years after the base year, for which there is no reported data (e.g. 2025 and 2026 are inflation adjusted from the 2024 base year).

To learn more about the methodology behind Cornerstone EEIO refer to 

the IO model, 

the GHG extension and 

Calculating the emission factors.

Cornerstone EEIO 2026 combines USEEIO’s detailed picture of the US economy with CEDA’s global coverage and trade modeling, representing a step change improvement to both models.

Three groups of improvements sit behind the changes.

A more current picture of the US economy that accounts for imports. US input-output tables are rebuilt for every year from 2017 to 2024, manufacturing uses facility-reported emissions, and imports are modeled where they are made.

Newer data for Europe, the UK and China, and better gap-filling for the rest. Europe moves from the OECD’s ICIO tables to Eurostat’s FIGARO (through 2023). China moves to the latest National Bureau of Statistics tables (through 2023), with more sectors. Countries without data are filled with the auto-balanced structural reflection method.

A validation process that feeds back into the model. Third-party benchmarks review the sectors behind about 50% of global emissions. Gaps are traced and fixed in the data or the method and documented when unresolved.

Together these make the 2017–2026 time series possible.
They translate real world changes to corporate footprints. Three examples show how:

Cornerstone adopts the most recent economic data released by the Chinese National Bureau of Statistics (2023 vs. 2020), which reflects methodology changes, changes in the economic structure, and sector-specific decarbonization.

For example, China’s battery factor rises by ~30% driven by a change in the composition of battery production in China. From 2020 to 2023, battery production more than tripled, but more importantly it shifted to require more Lithium-ion and less Lead-acid as inputs. This is because the majority of the market growth in batteries are in EVs and grid storage that require lithium-ion. Lithium-ion needs lithium chemicals and power-hungry cell factories, being more carbon intensive per dollar than lead-acid batteries, driving the emission factor up.



Figure 1:China battery production, 2020 and 2023. Output in GWh. The split by battery type is approximate. Sources: NBS input-output tables 2020 and 2023; MIIT; China lead-acid battery industry statistics.

Cornerstone adopts the most recent release of FIGARO, Eurostat’s official input-output and emissions dataset. FIGARO is more granular than the OECD dataset for Europe, is available as a time series through 2023, and is updated every year, matching Cornerstone’s release cadence.

This data update lowers European factors by about 4% in median. The most significant change is in electricity factors, which fall in every EU country. This change is driven by an increase in renewable energy and by an increase in energy prices due to the gas-supply shocks the Ukraine war has caused in Europe. For example, Germany’s power factor fell by 60%, as renewables grew from 35% to over 50% of generation and wholesale power prices more than doubled.



Figure 2:Germany’s power emission factor falls by 60%. About 25% of the change comes from a cleaner grid, as renewables grew from 35% to over 50% of generation, and about 75% from higher prices, as wholesale power prices more than doubled, from about €44 to €95 per MWh. Sources: Ember, Öko-Institut, SMARD, Vattenfall.

hierarchy.lvl3: Incorporation of imports in the US
Incorporation of imports in the US

records.content:
USEEIO treated the US as a closed economy: every product used in the US was assumed to be made in the US. Cornerstone uses trade data to model each import in the country that produced it. Many imports come from more emissions-intensive economies such as China and India, so US factors tend to rise by 10 to 30% on average. This is the main upward pressure and the main reason for the change for USEEIO users. One example is light trucks and utility vehicles. The US factor rises by ~24%, mostly because many of their components are now modeled as imports from the countries that make them. Public data suggests that about 60% of the components of a US-assembled light truck are imported, with Mexico the largest source, followed by Europe and Canada (see 

Figure 3).



Figure 3:Estimated origin of the components of a US-assembled light truck. Sources: 

NHTSA AALA parts content data; 

International Trade Administration data as reported by MNI (March 2025).

records.content:
Structural reflection is the method CEDA uses to maintain the same sectoral granularity across all countries.

The ABSR method is an improvement in this methodology. It achieves two goals that are hard to deliver together in a global model:

All countries share the same 405 sectors, so emission factors compare like for like.

Each economy balances production and consumption in terms of monetary transactions and emissions.



Figure 5:How ABSR works. ABSR disaggregates each country’s economy into the same 405 sectors and balances it, so that production and consumption match in both money and emissions.

Cornerstone uses benchmark data built from about 1,000 sources to review the key sectors that drive about 50% of global emissions. Each review ends in one of three outcomes:

Sharper benchmark. Scope and price assumptions are aligned, so the external reference is directly comparable to the model.

Model improvement. The gap is traced to a data source or an allocation method, and fixed with more data or a corrected implementation.

Known discrepancy. The difference is documented, because of a limitation in how the model is built or a gap in the data.
